text: Accessibility Accessibility Statement Irving Health and Wellness Clinic wants every patient to be able to read our pages, book a visit, and contact us without barriers. We are working to make irvingwellnessclinic.com conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA. Call (972) 891-8650 Email info@irvingwellnessclinic.com What we have done These measures were applied in August 2026 after a full audit with axe-core in a real browser and manual keyboard checks. We re-test after every change. Colour contrast Text and button colours meet the 4.5 to 1 minimum, including links inside articles and on dark green sections. Keyboard access Every link, button, and form field shows a visible focus ring. A skip link jumps past the header on every page. Heading order Each page has one main heading and a logical heading order, so screen readers announce the structure in sequence. Text alternatives Images that carry meaning have alt text. Decorative images are hidden from screen readers. No moving content Review carousels no longer play on their own, so text does not move while you read it. Ongoing testing We audit the site after changes and act on accessibility reports within two business days. How to report a problem If a page, document, or feature is hard to use, tell us. Here is what happens next. 1 Tell us what happened Call (972) 891-8650, Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, or email info@irvingwellnessclinic.com. Include the web address, a short description, and the assistive technology you were using. 2 We reply within two business days A team member confirms the report and books your visit or answers your question another way, by phone if that is easier. 3 We fix and re-test Confirmed problems are corrected as quickly as we can, then the page is re-tested with automated tools and a keyboard pass. Questions about this statement Which standard does the clinic follow? We follow the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA, published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). These guidelines explain how to make web content usable for people who use screen readers, keyboard navigation, or magnification. Is the website fully compliant? No website can promise that. Our pages are partially conformant with WCAG 2.1 Level AA: the main pages pass automated and keyboard testing, and some third-party parts do not. We keep testing and fixing, and this page is updated when the site changes. What are the known limitations? The online booking calendar (Google Calendar), the contact form (LeadConnector), and the embedded map are provided by third parties and may not fully meet WCAG 2.1 AA. If you cannot use one of them, call or email us and we will book or answer for you. What are my rights? Irving Health and Wellness Clinic is a private practice. Nothing on this page changes your rights under the Americans with Disabilities Act or Texas law. Need help using this site? Call us during clinic hours and we will book your visit or answer your question by phone. Visit us at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 100, Irving, TX 75063. Call (972) 891-8650 Contact Us

mainEntity.name: Is Skinvive the same as a skin booster?

acceptedAnswer.text: Skin booster is the generic category name used internationally. Skinvive is the specific product that holds the FDA approval in the US, which matters because approval means the claims were tested against a placebo.

mainEntity.name: How soon will you see results?

acceptedAnswer.text: Expect the visible improvement to build over a few weeks as hydration improves, rather than an instant change on the day. Judge it at the one-month mark.

mainEntity.name: Does Skinvive help with acne scars or pores?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can soften the look of fine texture, but it does not treat scarring. Depressed acne scars respond better to microneedling, which works by rebuilding collagen rather than adding hydration.

mainEntity.name: Skinvive or Botox for smoother skin?

acceptedAnswer.text: They do different jobs. Botox relaxes the muscles that crease the skin, while Skinvive hydrates the skin itself. Lines caused by expression need Botox; texture and dullness point to Skinvive.

text: Skinvive vs Dermal Filler: Which One Do You Actually Need? By Irving H&W Clinic July 28, 2026 Medical Aesthetics Table of Contents Key Takeaways: Skinvive improves skin quality and hydration. It does not add volume. Dermal fillers restore lost volume and reshape features. Many people assume they need filler when their actual concern is skin texture. Skinvive gets called “a filler” constantly, including by people selling it. It is not one, and the confusion leads people to book the wrong treatment. Both are hyaluronic acid injectables. What they do with that hyaluronic acid is completely different, and that difference decides which one you need. What is Skinvive and how is it different from filler? Skinvive by Juvederm is a hyaluronic acid microdroplet injectable. The FDA approved it in May 2023 to improve skin smoothness of the cheeks in adults over 21, and it was the first product of its kind approved in the US. Rather than filling a specific line or hollow, it is placed as many tiny droplets across the treatment area. The goal is hydration, elasticity, and surface smoothness rather than shape. Does Skinvive add volume to the face? No. This is the single most important thing to understand about it. The droplets are too small and placed too superficially to lift or plump anything. If your concern is a deep fold, a flat cheek, or a thin lip, Skinvive is the wrong tool no matter how well it is marketed. Skinvive vs dermal filler: side by side The two products solve different problems, which the table makes clear. Skinvive Dermal filler What it does Hydrates, smooths skin surface Restores volume, reshapes features Placement Many microdroplets, superficial Targeted deeper placement Visible change Glow and texture, subtle Structural, visible in shape Best for Dull, crepey, dehydrated skin Folds, hollows, lips, contour Duration Up to 6 months Varies by product and area Price here $700 per syringe $800 for 1 syringe, $1,520 for 2 The practical question at consultation is simple. Is the issue the surface of your skin, or the shape underneath it? What skin concerns does Skinvive treat? It suits skin that looks tired rather than sunken. Dullness, fine crepey texture, and dehydration that skincare alone has not fixed. In the clinical study behind the approval, patients reported higher satisfaction with how glowing, hydrated, refreshed, and healthy their skin looked. Those words describe surface quality, not shape, which is exactly the product’s lane. “One key way to improve skin quality is by enhancing hydration. SKINVIVE by JUVEDERM is truly innovative because it works beneath the skin’s surface to increase skin hydration improving skin quality,” said Macrene Alexiades, MD, PhD, dual US-EU board-certified dermatologist and lead investigator of the Skinvive clinical trial, in AbbVie’s approval announcement . How is Skinvive injected? It is placed as a series of very small injections spaced roughly half a centimeter to a centimeter apart across the cheeks. The appointment is quick, and downtime is minimal. Expect small raised bumps at the injection points that settle within a day or two, and the usual chance of minor bruising. How long does Skinvive last? Up to six months with optimal treatment. Repeat sessions maintain the effect. That is shorter than most volumizing fillers, which is consistent with how superficially it sits and how it is metabolized. Can you get Skinvive and filler in the same visit? Yes, and the combination makes sense more often than either alone. They are complementary because they work at different depths on different problems. A common plan treats lost volume with filler first, then uses Skinvive for surface quality. Our dermal fillers page covers the volume side in detail. Is Skinvive approved for the neck? In June 2026 the FDA approved Skinvive for the appearance of neck lines, making it the first hyaluronic acid injectable with that indication. It is a genuinely new development in an area that previously had few good injectable options. Our clinic currently offers Skinvive for its cheek indication. If neck treatment is something you are interested in, ask at consultation and we will tell you honestly whether and when we offer it. What are the side effects of Skinvive? The common reactions are local and short-lived. Small bumps at the injection points for a day or two Redness, tenderness, or minor bruising Temporary unevenness while the droplets settle Can it be reversed? Yes. Like other hyaluronic acid products, it can be dissolved with hyaluronidase if ever needed, which is part of why HA injectables are considered a lower-risk category. Who is a good candidate for Skinvive? Someone whose skin looks dull or crepey but whose facial volume is fine. Often that is a person in their late twenties to forties who is not ready for filler and does not need it. It also suits filler patients who have volume handled and want the skin itself to match. It is not a substitute for treating deep folds or significant volume loss. How much does Skinvive cost? Skinvive is $700 per syringe at our Irving clinic. Dermal fillers are $800 for one syringe and $1,520 for two. If you are unsure which you need, book a consultation before committing to either. The consultation is free, and choosing the wrong product is not. Frequently Asked Questions Is Skinvive the same as a skin booster? Skin booster is the generic category name used internationally. Skinvive is the specific product that holds the FDA approval in the US, which matters because approval means the claims were tested against a placebo. How soon will you see results? Expect the visible improvement to build over a few weeks as hydration improves, rather than an instant change on the day. Judge it at the one-month mark. Does Skinvive help with acne scars or pores? It can soften the look of fine texture, but it does not treat scarring. Depressed acne scars respond better to microneedling , which works by rebuilding collagen rather than adding hydration. Skinvive or Botox for smoother skin? They do different jobs. Botox relaxes the muscles that crease the skin, while Skinvive hydrates the skin itself. Lines caused by expression need Botox ; texture and dullness point to Skinvive. Which one do you actually need? If the shape of your face has changed, that is a filler conversation. If the shape is fine but the skin surface looks tired, that is Skinvive. Plenty of people need neither yet, and we will say so. Book through our aesthetic treatments page or call 972-891-8650 and we will look at your skin before recommending anything. text: How Many Laser Hair Removal Sessions Do You Need? Area by Area By Irving H&W Clinic July 27, 2026 Medical Aesthetics Table of Contents Key Takeaways: Most people need six to nine sessions for best results, not one or two. Sessions are spaced roughly six weeks apart because only growing hairs respond. Laser gives permanent hair reduction, not permanent removal. The single most common surprise with laser hair removal is the number of visits. People book expecting one session and a smooth result. That is not how the hair growth cycle works, and understanding why makes the schedule and the pricing make sense. How many laser hair removal sessions do most people need? Most people need six to nine treatments for the best result, according to the American Society for Laser Medicine and Surgery. Some see good clearance at four to six. Cleveland Clinic puts the typical course at four to six sessions spaced six weeks apart, which can take up to nine months from start to finish. Why does laser hair removal take more than one session? The laser only works on hair that is actively growing. Hair in its resting or shedding phase has no pigment connection to the follicle for the laser to target. At any given moment only a portion of the hair in an area is in that growth phase. Each session catches whatever is growing that day, which is why the course is spread out. How far apart should sessions be scheduled? Around six weeks for most body areas. Facial hair cycles faster and is often treated every four weeks. Going sooner wastes a session, because the next batch of follicles has not entered the growth phase yet. Going much later is less of a problem, though it can stretch the total timeline. How many sessions for legs, underarms, bikini, and face? Coarse, dense hair on the body tends to respond faster than fine or hormonally driven hair on the face. Area Typical sessions Spacing Underarms 6 to 8 Every 6 weeks Bikini or Brazilian 6 to 8 Every 6 weeks Lower legs 6 to 8 Every 6 to 8 weeks Back or chest 8 or more Every 6 to 8 weeks Face, upper lip or chin 8 or more Every 4 weeks The American Academy of Dermatology lists the chest, back, shoulders, neck, bikini line and face as suitable areas, with the exception of skin around the eyes. Does hair color change how many sessions you need? Yes, more than almost any other factor. The laser targets pigment in the follicle, so dark coarse hair responds best. Grey, white, red and very blonde hair have little pigment to absorb the light. Laser is generally not effective on those, regardless of how many sessions you book. Does skin tone affect laser hair removal? It affects which device is appropriate rather than whether you are a candidate. Modern systems safely treat a wide range of skin tones when settings and wavelength are matched correctly. This is one of the clearest arguments for having it done in a medical setting rather than wherever is cheapest. “Because of its popularity, laser hair removal might seem like a procedure that anyone can do, but in the wrong hands, it can cause serious skin damage,” says Carolyn I. Jacob, MD, FAAD, board-certified dermatologist and Associate Clinical Instructor of Dermatology at Northwestern’s Feinberg School of Medicine, in an American Academy of Dermatology news release . How much hair is gone after the first session? Expect a 10% to 25% reduction after the first treatment, per the American Academy of Dermatology. Results build with each subsequent session. Shedding in the one to three weeks after a session is normal and is often mistaken for regrowth. Is laser hair removal permanent? It gives permanent hair reduction, not permanent removal. That distinction matters and is often blurred in advertising. Treated follicles that are destroyed do not regrow. Some follicles survive, and hormonal changes can activate new ones later, so most people need occasional maintenance. Do you need maintenance sessions? Usually one or two a year after finishing the initial course. Some people need none for years. Hormonal shifts from pregnancy, menopause, or conditions such as PCOS can trigger new growth. Our guide to PCOS root causes covers why that happens. What should you do before and after a session? Preparation changes your result more than most people expect. Shave the area the day before, since the laser needs the follicle intact below the skin Do not wax, pluck or thread for four weeks beforehand, as that removes the target Avoid sun exposure and self-tanner before and after treatment What about aftercare? Expect redness and slight bumps for a day or two. Skip hot tubs, saunas and heavy workouts for 24 hours, and use sunscreen on any exposed treated area. “If you experience any pain or discoloration after receiving laser hair removal, see a board-certified dermatologist right away,” Jacob advises in the same release. text: Double Chin Treatment Without Surgery: How Kybella Works and Who It Suits By Irving H&W Clinic July 27, 2026 Medical Aesthetics Table of Contents Key Takeaways: Kybella is an injectable that destroys fat cells under the chin, and it is the only FDA-approved drug for that use. Most people need more than one session, spaced at least a month apart. Swelling after treatment is expected and is part of how it works. A double chin is stubborn in a way that frustrates people. It often stays put through weight loss, and it shows up in photos from angles nobody chooses. This guide covers what actually causes submental fat, how the non-surgical options compare, and who Kybella suits. What causes a double chin? Submental fat sits in a pocket beneath the jawline. Genetics decide how much you store there and how visible it is. Weight gain adds to it, but weight is not the whole story. Plenty of lean people have one, and plenty of people lose weight everywhere except under the chin. Age contributes too, since skin loses elasticity and the area softens. What are the non-surgical options for submental fat? There are three broad routes. An injectable that destroys the fat cells, a device that freezes them, and surgery that removes them. Only one of those is a drug approved specifically for this area. Our clinic offers the injectable route, which is Kybella. How does Kybella break down fat under the chin? Kybella is deoxycholic acid. Your body already makes it, and its normal job is helping you absorb dietary fat. Injected into a fat pocket, it works as a cytolytic drug. It physically breaks down the fat cell membrane, and the destroyed cells are cleared by the body over the following weeks. Is Kybella FDA approved? Yes. The FDA approved it in April 2015 for moderate to severe fat below the chin in adults. Approval was based on two placebo-controlled Phase III trials involving more than 1,000 adults. It remains the only injectable approved for this specific use. How many Kybella treatments will you need? More than one, in almost every case. The FDA label allows up to six treatments, spaced at least one month apart. In the clinical trials, 59% of patients received all six. Your provider maps the area and decides the number based on how much fat is there and how you respond to the first round. What happens during a Kybella appointment? The area is marked with a grid so the injections are evenly spaced. Numbing is applied first, and ice helps with comfort. The label permits up to 50 small injections in a single session. The injecting itself takes around 15 to 20 minutes. What does Kybella recovery look like? Swelling is not a side effect here so much as evidence the drug is doing its job. It is the most noticeable part of recovery. Stage What to expect First 24 hours Swelling begins, area feels tender and warm Days 2 to 4 Swelling usually peaks, chin may look fuller than before Week 1 to 2 Swelling settles, firm lumps under the skin are common Weeks 3 to 4 Most visible swelling resolves, firmness fades After 1 month Earliest point a further session is permitted Timelines vary between people. Plan your first session well ahead of any event you care about. How does Kybella compare to fat freezing and a neck lift? Each targets the same fat with a different mechanism, cost, and downtime. Kybella Fat freezing Neck lift Type Injectable drug Cooling device Surgery Anesthesia Topical numbing None General or local Sessions Up to 6 Usually 1 to 3 One procedure Downtime Swelling for days to weeks Minimal Weeks Treats loose skin No No Yes Offered here Yes No No If loose skin rather than fat is the main issue, none of the fat treatments will fix it. That is worth establishing at consultation before you spend anything. Are Kybella results permanent? The treated fat cells are destroyed and do not come back. In that sense the result is lasting. You can still gain weight, and the remaining cells in the area can enlarge. Most people who keep their weight stable do not need repeat rounds. What are the side effects of Kybella? Most reactions are local and temporary. The trial data gives useful numbers rather than vague reassurance. Bruising affected 72% of trial subjects Swelling, pain, numbness, and firmness at the site are common Nerve injury causing an uneven smile occurred in 4%, and every case resolved on its own How long did the rarer effects last? In the trials, nerve-related weakness resolved with a median of 44 days. Difficulty swallowing occurred in 2% of subjects and resolved with a median of 3 days. Who is not a good candidate for Kybella? It is not for everyone. The label specifically warns against use where infection is present at the injection site. Anyone with a current or previous history of difficulty swallowing should avoid it, since treatment can worsen that. It is also not appropriate if your concern is loose skin rather than fat. How much does Kybella cost? Kybella is $600 per treatment at our Irving clinic. Because most people need several sessions, budget for the full course rather than one visit. Insurance does not cover it, since it is a cosmetic treatment. We give you an expected session count at consultation so the total is clear upfront. Frequently Asked Questions Does Kybella tighten loose skin? No. It treats fat only. If skin laxity is the main issue, a fat treatment will not improve it and may make it more noticeable. This is the single most common reason we tell someone Kybella is not right for them. How soon will you see results? Most people see a visible change after two to four treatments. Because swelling masks the result early on, judge progress about a month after each session rather than in the first week. Does Kybella hurt? There is stinging and burning during the injections and for a short time afterward. Numbing cream and ice make it manageable. Most people describe it as uncomfortable rather than severe. Can Kybella be used elsewhere on the body? Fat below the chin is the only FDA-approved use. Anything else is off-label, and we do not offer it that way. Can you combine Kybella with other treatments? Yes, though usually not on the same day. Many people pair it with Botox or dermal fillers for the wider jawline and lower face. Is Kybella right for you? It suits people close to their goal weight with a defined pocket of fat under the chin and reasonable skin quality. It does not suit people whose main concern is sagging. The honest test is a consultation where someone examines the area and tells you which of the two you have. Book through our aesthetic treatments page or call 972-891-8650. text: NAD+ IV Therapy Benefits: What the Research Shows and What It Does Not By Irving H&W Clinic July 27, 2026 IV Therapy Table of Contents Key Takeaways: NAD+ is a coenzyme your cells use for energy production and DNA repair, and levels fall with age. IV delivery puts NAD+ straight into your bloodstream, bypassing digestion entirely. Controlled human data on IV NAD+ specifically is still limited to small pilot studies. NAD+ is the most expensive drip on most clinic menus, and the most oversold. Plenty of pages promise reversed aging and restored energy, while far fewer explain what the research has actually tested. What is NAD+ and what does it do in the body? NAD+ stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. It is a coenzyme found in every living cell, and your body cannot make energy without it. It shuttles electrons during metabolism and supports the enzymes that repair damaged DNA. NAD+ levels decline as people age. That observation is what drove the interest in replacing it. What are the benefits of NAD+ IV therapy? Clinics most often offer NAD+ for low energy, brain fog, burnout, and recovery after illness. Patients frequently report feeling clearer and more energetic in the days after a session. Those reports matter, but they are not the same as trial evidence. The honest position is that the mechanism is well understood while the clinical outcomes are still being studied. Does NAD+ IV therapy actually work? It reliably does one thing: it raises circulating NAD+ levels. That much is measurable and not in dispute. Whether raising those levels produces durable improvements in energy, cognition, or aging is not yet settled. Most published human research studies oral precursors rather than IV infusions, so the evidence does not transfer cleanly. What does the research actually show? Separating the established from the promising is the most useful thing this page can do. Claim Evidence status Source NAD+ is essential to cellular energy and DNA repair Established biochemistry Clinical Evidence for Targeting NAD Therapeutically, NIH PMC NAD+ levels decline with age Well documented NIH PMC review IV infusion raises circulating NAD+ Demonstrated, small pilot trials Randomized placebo-controlled IV NAD+ pilot, medRxiv NAD+ shows promise in neurodegeneration and inflammation Promising, not proven in humans Nature Aging review, 2025 NAD+ IV reverses aging or treats disease Not supported No adequate human trials A 2025 review in Nature Aging , co-authored by more than 25 researchers, named NAD+ biology one of the more promising directions in aging research. The same review was clear that clinical proof in humans is still pending. Why is NAD+ given by IV instead of a pill? Anything you swallow has to survive stomach acid and liver processing before it reaches your bloodstream. A meaningful share is lost along the way. An infusion skips that path completely, which is why clinics use it when the goal is to raise levels quickly. The same logic applies across our IV therapy menu. NAD+ IV drip vs NAD+ injection: which one fits your goal? Both deliver NAD+ past the digestive system. They differ in dose, time, and cost. NAD+ IV drip NAD+ injection Dose 250mg or 500mg 25mg to 200mg Price $325 or $475 $50 Time in clinic Longer, dose dependent Minutes Best for A full loading dose, first-time protocols Topping up between infusions, tighter budgets Most people starting out do a small number of infusions first, then use injections to maintain. How long does a NAD+ infusion take? Longer than a standard vitamin drip. NAD+ has to run slowly, and the higher the dose the longer the session. Rushing it is what causes discomfort, so the drip rate is set to your tolerance rather than the clock. Your provider will give you an expected time for your specific dose when you book. What does a NAD+ drip feel like? Most people notice a flushing sensation, some warmth in the chest, or mild nausea if the drip runs too fast. It is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. The fix is simple. Slowing the infusion resolves it within a minute or two, which is why NAD+ is never rushed. What are the side effects of NAD+ IV therapy? Common effects are infusion related and stop when the session ends. Flushing, warmth, or chest tightness during the drip Nausea or cramping if the rate is too fast Bruising or soreness at the IV site Is long-term use well studied? Long-term safety data for repeated high-dose NAD+ infusions is limited. A 2026 pilot study in Frontiers in Aging tracking real-world infusions reported abdominal cramping, nausea, increased heart rate, and chest pressure during NAD+ drips, and found infusions of the precursor NR were better tolerated. That is another reason to treat it as supportive care rather than a standing prescription. Who should not get NAD+ IV therapy? NAD+ infusions are not appropriate for everyone. Skip it or seek specific clearance if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have kidney or heart failure, or are being treated for an active cancer. Anyone on multiple prescription medications should have a provider review the plan first. Our intake includes a medical screen for exactly this reason. How often should you get NAD+ IV therapy? There is no evidence-backed universal schedule. Clinics commonly run a short series of infusions close together, then move to spaced maintenance. The sensible approach is to treat the first series as a trial and judge by how you actually feel. Our guide on how often to get IV vitamin therapy covers the same reasoning across drip types. How much does NAD+ IV therapy cost? NAD+ 250mg is $325 and NAD+ 500mg is $475. A NAD+ injection ranging from 25mg to 200mg is $50. Insurance does not cover wellness infusions. Given the cost, it is worth ruling out cheaper explanations for low energy first, including sleep, thyroid function, and B12 status. Frequently Asked Questions Is NAD+ IV therapy FDA approved? No. NAD+ is not approved as a drug to treat aging, fatigue, or any specific condition. It is used in wellness settings, which is a different regulatory category and a reason to be cautious about strong claims. Can you take an NAD+ supplement instead? Oral precursors such as NR and NMN are widely sold and carry most of the published human research. They raise NAD+ more slowly than an infusion. For many people they are a reasonable and far cheaper starting point. How soon would you feel a difference? Some people report a lift within a day or two. Others notice nothing after a full series. Because the response varies this much, we suggest judging it after a defined trial rather than committing to a long protocol upfront. Is NAD+ safe to use long term? Unknown. Short-term infusions appear well tolerated in the studies published so far, but there is no good long-term safety data on repeated high doses. Will NAD+ help my fatigue? It might, if your fatigue has a metabolic component. It will not correct fatigue caused by poor sleep, thyroid disease, anemia, or a hormone imbalance. Our guide to IV therapy for chronic fatigue walks through those causes. Is NAD+ worth trying? It depends on what you expect from it. As a supportive option for energy and recovery, alongside sleep, labs, and nutrition, it is reasonable to try with clear expectations. As a treatment for aging or a substitute for a diagnosis, the evidence does not support it. If you want to talk it through, book a consultation or call 972-891-8650. text: Not Losing Weight on Semaglutide? 5 Research-Backed Reasons and Fixes By Irving H&W Clinic July 21, 2026 Medical Weight Loss Table of Contents Key takeaway: A stalled scale on semaglutide is common and usually fixable. The most frequent causes are a dose that never reached its effective level, a natural plateau that arrives after months of steady loss, habits the medication cannot override, or biology that responds better to a different medication. Each one has a specific, evidence-backed fix. Semaglutide has better trial results than almost anything that came before it. It is also not magic. In the landmark STEP 1 trial of 1,961 adults, participants on weekly 2.4 mg semaglutide lost 14.9% of their body weight on average over 68 weeks. But inside that average sits a quieter number: 86.4% of participants lost at least 5% of their weight, which means roughly 1 in 7 did not. If your progress has stalled, you are not imagining it, and you are not alone. Here is what the research says is actually going on. Is Your Semaglutide Dose High Enough? The trial results people quote came from the full 2.4 mg weekly dose, reached after 16 weeks of step-up increases. Many stalled patients turn out to be sitting at an early titration dose, sometimes for months. The medication is working exactly as expected; it simply was never raised to the level that produced the famous numbers. This is the first thing to review with your provider. If side effects blocked earlier increases, a slower ramp or a different escalation schedule often gets you the rest of the way. Our semaglutide program reviews dose against progress every month for exactly this reason. When Does Weight Loss Plateau on Semaglutide? In STEP 1, average weight loss flattened in the final months of the 68-week trial. That plateau is not failure. It is the body reaching a new equilibrium: as you lose weight, you burn fewer calories at rest, appetite signals adapt, and the same dose now maintains rather than reduces. The distinction that matters is timing. A plateau after 8 to 12 months of steady loss is physiology. A stall in the first 3 months, at a full dose, is a signal to look deeper at the causes below. 3 Habits That Stall Weight Loss on Semaglutide Semaglutide quiets appetite. It does not choose what you eat, lift weights for you, or put you to bed on time. Three habits show up over and over in stalled patients: Too little protein. Eating much less overall means protein needs jump proportionally. Low protein accelerates muscle loss, which drags your resting metabolism down with it. No resistance training. A meaningful share of rapid weight loss can come from lean mass. Muscle is the tissue that keeps your calorie burn up after the loss, and strength training is how you keep it. Short sleep and unmanaged stress. Both push hunger hormones in the wrong direction and quietly raise intake. The habits that protect weight loss long-term are the same ones that break plateaus. Medical Reasons Semaglutide Stops Working Weight is regulated by overlapping hormone systems, and a stall is sometimes the first visible sign of one of them. Untreated insulin resistance , thyroid dysfunction, and sex-hormone imbalances can all blunt progress on a GLP-1 medication. This is why a labs-first program matters: bloodwork drawn before and during treatment tells you whether the plateau is behavioral, pharmacologic, or hormonal. Semaglutide Non-Responders: When Switching Makes Sense True non-response is real, and the researchers who ran the biggest trials say so plainly. “Even though drugs like tirzepatide and semaglutide work really well, better than anything we have ever seen, we still have people who don’t respond to them. So, moving forward, we want to keep trying to do better.” Dr. Louis Aronne, Comprehensive Weight Control Center | Weill Cornell Medicine Non-response to semaglutide does not predict non-response to everything. In the 72-week head-to-head trial, tirzepatide produced 20.2% average weight loss versus 13.7% for semaglutide, and twice as many participants reached a 25% reduction. Patients who plateau on semaglutide sometimes see renewed progress after a supervised switch to tirzepatide , which works on two hormone receptors instead of one. The full comparison is in our semaglutide vs tirzepatide breakdown . How to Restart Weight Loss on Semaglutide Confirm your current dose and how long you have been on it. Below full dose, the next step is usually titration, not switching. Track body composition, not just the scale. Losing fat while holding muscle can read as a “stall” on a bathroom scale. Audit protein, strength training, and sleep for two honest weeks before concluding the medication stopped working. Get labs if you have not had them since starting. Thyroid, fasting insulin, and HbA1c can each explain a plateau. If you are at full dose with clean labs and honest habits, ask your provider about a supervised switch. That conversation is a normal part of good care, not a failure. FAQs How long should I wait before deciding semaglutide is not working? Give the medication a fair trial at a therapeutic dose. Most providers look for at least 5% weight loss after roughly 3 months at full dose. Stalling during early titration weeks is normal and not a verdict on the medication. Is it normal to stop losing weight after a year? Yes. Trial data shows average loss flattening near the end of the first year as the body reaches a new set point. At that stage the goal shifts from losing to maintaining, which is a success, not a stall. Will increasing the dose restart my weight loss? Sometimes, if you are below the full therapeutic dose. That decision belongs with your provider, because it depends on your current dose, side effects, and labs. Never adjust a GLP-1 dose on your own. Should I switch to tirzepatide if semaglutide stalled? It is one evidence-backed option among several. The head-to-head trial favored tirzepatide on every weight measure, but dose, habits, and underlying conditions should be ruled out first. A supervised transition keeps side effects predictable if you do switch. Get Your Plateau Properly Evaluated A plateau is information, not defeat. Our medical weight loss program in Irving treats it that way: labs, body composition, dose history, and habits reviewed together, then a specific next step instead of a shrug. text: Hormone Pellets vs Injections vs Creams: Pros, Cons, and How to Choose By Irving H&W Clinic July 21, 2026 Hormone Replacement Therapy Table of Contents Quick answer: Pellets give the steadiest hormone levels and need attention only every 3 to 4 months, but the dose cannot be changed once implanted. Injections are inexpensive and easy to adjust, but levels rise and fall between doses. Creams are gentle and flexible, but daily and easy to forget. The right fit depends on your labs, your schedule, and how your body responds. If you have decided to explore hormone therapy , the next question surprises most people. It is not “which hormone?” Your labs answer that. It is “how should it get into your body?” Pellets, injections, and creams can all deliver the same bioidentical hormones. What changes is the rhythm: how steady your levels stay, how often you think about dosing, and how quickly your provider can correct course. How Hormone Pellets, Injections, and Creams Work All three methods exist to solve the same problem: your body expects hormones on a steady drip, not in bursts. Each method approximates that drip differently. Pellets are rice-sized cylinders placed under the skin of the hip in a short in-office procedure. They dissolve slowly and release hormones continuously for roughly 3 to 6 months. Injections deliver a depot of hormone into muscle or fat, typically every week or two for testosterone. Levels peak in the first days, then decline until the next dose. Creams and gels absorb through the skin daily. Levels follow your application habits, which makes consistency the whole game. Pellets vs Injections vs Creams: Comparison Chart Pellets Injections Creams / Gels Dosing rhythm Every 3 to 6 months Weekly to biweekly Daily Level stability Steadiest, no weekly swings Peak after the shot, trough before the next Steady if applied consistently Dose adjustability Lowest: cannot change until the pellet dissolves High: adjust at any dose Highest: adjust day to day Procedure involved Minor in-office insertion, small incision Quick needle stick None Common friction Insertion-site soreness, rare pellet extrusion Mood or energy dips before the next dose Skipped days, transfer to partners or children Who tends to prefer it People who want to stop thinking about dosing People who want control and lower cost Needle-averse patients starting low and slow Hormone Pellet Therapy: Pros and Cons The strongest argument for pellets is the absence of a cycle. There is no shot day, no pre-dose slump, no daily application to remember. For patients whose symptoms return every time they miss a dose, that steadiness is the entire point. The trade-off is commitment. Once a pellet is implanted, the dose is fixed until it dissolves. If your level runs high or side effects appear, there is no simple way to dial it back. That is why careful, conservative dosing from your baseline labs matters more with pellets than with any other method. It is also why the insertion should follow bloodwork, not a sales script. Hormone Injections: Pros and Cons Injections remain the workhorse of testosterone therapy for a reason. They are inexpensive, widely available in FDA-approved forms, and easy to fine-tune. If your 6-week labs show you are running high, next week’s dose simply comes down. The trade-off is the wave pattern. Levels climb after each shot and fall before the next one, and some patients feel that fall as fatigue, irritability, or low motivation. Splitting into smaller, more frequent doses flattens the wave for many people, which is exactly the kind of adjustment a monitored program can make. Hormone Creams and Gels: Pros and Cons Daily creams and gels produce the most physiologic rhythm of all when used perfectly, and they are the easiest to stop or adjust. They suit patients starting cautiously, and women managing perimenopause symptoms who want room to titrate slowly. The trade-offs are human ones. Absorption varies from person to person and day to day. Missed applications show up as symptom swings. And residue can transfer to partners, children, or pets through skin contact in the hours after application. Compounded vs FDA-Approved Hormones: What Medical Societies Say Delivery method is only half the question. The other half is whether the preparation itself is FDA-approved or custom-compounded, and the major societies have taken a clear position on that. The Endocrine Society and ACOG both recommend FDA-approved formulations whenever one exists, because compounded preparations are not tested for consistency the same way. “Pellets can cause high hormonal peaks and prolonged elevations, which are not well monitored.” Wender et al., peer-reviewed pellet safety review, 2025 | PubMed Central Note what that criticism targets: unmonitored dosing, more than the method itself. It is exactly why baseline labs, conservative starting doses, and scheduled rechecks matter more with pellets than with any other option. Dr. Stephanie Faubion, director of the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health, has cautioned that there is “no real benefit” and “potential harm” in unregulated hormone preparations. The practical takeaway is not that any single method is wrong. It is that formulation, dosing, and monitoring deserve the same scrutiny as the delivery route. Ask any provider which formulation they use, how the starting dose is set, and when your levels get rechecked. Good clinics answer all three without hesitation. How to Choose Between Pellets, Injections, and Creams How do you handle routines? If daily steps fail you, creams will too. If you dread appointments, pellet reinsertions may lapse. Match the method to your real habits, not your ideal ones. How much adjustment will you likely need? First-time patients often benefit from starting on an adjustable method, then switching to pellets once their effective dose is proven and stable. How do you respond to swings? If you feel every trough between injections, steadier delivery is worth prioritizing. Your symptom pattern between doses is data. Bring it to your provider. FAQs Do pellets work better than injections? Neither is universally better. Pellets deliver steadier levels with less effort, while injections offer more control and lower cost. Head-to-head, the deciding factors are your response, your schedule, and how much dose adjustment you need in the first months of therapy. How long do hormone pellets last? Most patients get roughly 3 to 4 months from testosterone pellets, and some closer to 6. Metabolism, activity level, and dose all affect the timeline. Symptoms returning early is a signal to recheck labs, not simply to implant a larger dose. Can I switch delivery methods later? Yes, and switching is common. Many patients start on injections or creams while their effective dose is being established, then move to pellets for convenience. The reverse also happens when someone wants finer control. Timing the switch around your labs keeps levels steady. Are hormone pellets FDA-approved? Some are, and some are not. An FDA-approved testosterone pellet exists for men, while many pellets, especially estradiol pellets for women, are custom-compounded. That is exactly why the Endocrine Society and ACOG advise asking which formulation you are getting before starting therapy. Get a Recommendation Built on Your Labs The honest answer to “which method is best” is always personal: it depends on your bloodwork, your symptoms, and your life. Our hormone therapy program in Irving starts with a full panel, walks through every delivery option, and monitors your levels after you choose, so the method serves the dose and not the other way around.
